{{Short description|Information theorem}}
{{Redirect|Blackwell order|other uses|Rao-Blackwell Theorem}}

In the mathematical subjects of [[information theory]] and [[decision theory]], '''Blackwell's informativeness theorem''' is an important result related to the ranking of information structures, or experiments. It states that there is an equivalence between three possible rankings of information structures: one based in ''[[expected utility]]'', one based in ''[[Blackwell's informativeness theorem#Garbling|informativeness]]'', and one based in ''[[Blackwell's informativeness theorem#Feasibility|feasibility]]''. This ranking defines a [[partial order]] over information structures known as the '''Blackwell order''', or '''Blackwell's criterion'''.<ref name = "oliveira" >{{cite journal |last1=de Oliveira |first1=Henrique |title=Blackwell's informativeness theorem using diagrams |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |date=2018 |volume=109 |pages=126–131 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2017.12.008 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825617302270|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name = "kosenko">{{cite arXiv | last = Kosenko| first = Andre| date = 2021 | title = Algebraic Properties of Blackwell's Order and A Cardinal Measure of Informativeness | eprint = 2110.11399 | class = econ.TH}}</ref>

The theorem states equivalent conditions under which any expected utility maximizing decision maker prefers information structure <math>\sigma </math> over <math>\sigma '</math>, for any decision problem. The result was first proven by [[David Blackwell]] in 1951, and generalized in 1953.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blackwell |first1=David |author1-link=David Blackwell |title=Comparison of Experiments |journal=Second Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability |date=1951 |page=2}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Blackwell |first1=David |title=Equivalent comparison of experiments |journal=The Annals of Mathematical Statistics |date=1953 |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=265–272|doi=10.1214/aoms/1177729032 }}</ref>

==Setting==

=== Decision making under uncertainty ===
A decision maker faces a set of possible states of the world <math>\Omega </math> and a set of possible actions <math>A </math> to take. For every <math>\omega \in \Omega </math> and <math>a \in A</math>, her utility is <math>u(a, \omega)</math>. She does not know the state of the world <math>\omega </math>, but has a [[prior probability]] <math>p : \Omega \rightarrow [0, 1]</math> for every possible state. For every action she takes, her expected utility is

:<math> \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} u(a, \omega) p(\omega) </math>

Given such prior <math> p </math>, she chooses an action <math> a \in A </math> to maximize her expected utility. We denote such maximum attainable utility (the [[expected value]] of taking the optimal action) by

:<math> V(p) = \underset{a \in A}\operatorname{max} \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} u(a, \omega) p (\omega) </math>

We refer to the data <math>(\Omega, A, u, p)</math> as a ''decision making problem''.

=== Information structures ===

An ''information structure'' (or an ''experiment'') can be seen as way to improve on the utility given by the prior, in the sense of providing more information to the decision maker. Formally, an information structure is a tuple <math>(S, \sigma)</math>, where <math>S</math> is a signal space and <math>\sigma : \Omega \rightarrow \Delta S</math> is a function which gives the conditional probability <math>\sigma(s | \omega)</math> of observing signal <math>s \in S </math> when the state of the world is <math>\omega</math>. An information structure can also be thought of as the setting of an experiment.

By observing the signal <math>s </math>, the decision maker can update her beliefs about the state of the world <math> \omega </math> via [[Bayes' rule]], giving the [[posterior probability]]

:<math> \pi (\omega | s) = \frac{p (\omega) \sigma(s | \omega)}{\pi (s)} </math>

where <math> \pi(s) := \sum_{\omega' \in \Omega} p (\omega') \sigma(s | \omega') </math>. By observing the signal <math> s </math> and updating her beliefs with the information structure <math>(S, \sigma)</math>, the decision maker's new expected utility value from taking the optimal action is

:<math> V(\pi, s) =  \underset{a \in A}\operatorname{max} \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} u(a, \omega) \pi (\omega | s) </math>

and the "expected value of <math>(S, \sigma)</math>" for the decision maker (i.e., the expected value of taking the optimal action under the information structure) is defined as

:<math> W(\sigma) = \sum_{s \in S} V(\pi, s) \pi (s)  </math>

=== Garbling ===

If two information structures <math> (S, \sigma) </math> and <math> (S', \sigma') </math> have the same underlying signal space, we abuse some notation and refer to <math> \sigma </math> and <math> \sigma' </math> as information structures themselves. We say that <math> \sigma' </math> is a '''garbling''' of <math> \sigma </math> if there exists a [[Markov kernel| stochastic map]]<ref name = "oliveira"></ref> (for finite signal spaces <math>S</math> and <math>S'</math>, a [[Markov matrix]]) <math>\gamma : S \times S' \rightarrow [0, 1] </math> such that:

:<math>\sigma'(s' | w) = \sum_{s \in S} \gamma(s, s') \sigma(s | w) \quad \wedge \quad \sum_{s' \in S'}\gamma(s, s') = 1.</math>

Intuitively, garbling is a way of adding "noise" to an information structure, such that the garbled information structure is considered to be less informative.

=== Feasibility ===

A '''[[Strategy (game theory)#Pure and mixed strategies|mixed strategy]]''' in the context of a decision-making problem is a function <math>\alpha : S \rightarrow \Delta A</math> which gives, for every signal <math>s \in S</math>, a probability distribution <math> \alpha(a | s) </math> over possible actions in <math>A</math>. With the information structure <math> (S, \sigma) </math>, a strategy <math> \alpha</math> induces a distribution over actions <math>\alpha_{\sigma}( a |\omega)</math> conditional on the state of the world <math> \omega </math>, given by the mapping

:<math> \omega \mapsto \alpha_{\sigma}( a |\omega)= \sum_{s \in S} \alpha (a | s) \sigma (s | \omega) \in \Delta A</math>

That is, <math>\alpha_{\sigma}( a |\omega)</math> gives the probability of taking action <math>a \in A</math> given that the state of the world is <math>\omega \in  \Omega</math> under information structure <math> (S, \sigma) </math> – notice that this is nothing but a [[convex combination]] of the <math> \alpha(a | s) </math> with weights <math>\sigma (s | \omega)</math>. We say that <math>\alpha_{\sigma}( a |\omega)</math> is a ''feasible'' strategy (or conditional probability over actions) under <math> (S, \sigma) </math>.

Given an information structure <math> (S, \sigma) </math>, let

:<math> \Phi_{\sigma} = \{\alpha_{\sigma}( a | \omega)  </math> |&nbsp; <math> \alpha : S \rightarrow \Delta A\}</math>

be the set of all conditional probabilities over
actions (i.e., strategies) that are feasible under <math> (S, \sigma) </math>.

Given two information structures  <math> (S, \sigma) </math> and  <math> (S, \sigma') </math>, we say that <math>\sigma</math> ''yields a larger set of feasible strategies'' than <math>\sigma'</math> if

:<math> \Phi_{\sigma'} \subset \Phi_{\sigma}</math>

==Statement==

Blackwell's theorem states that, given two information structures <math> \sigma </math> and <math> \sigma' </math>, the following are equivalent:<ref name = "oliveira" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Karni |first1=Edi |last2=Safra |first2=Zvi |author1-link=Edi Karni |title=Hybrid decision model and the ranking of experiments |journal=Journal of Mathematical Economics |date=2022 |volume=101 |article-number=102700 |doi=10.1016/j.jmateco.2022.102700 |s2cid=237370357 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304406822000489|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

# <math> W(\sigma') \leq W (\sigma) </math> for any decision-making problem <math> (\Omega, A, u, p) </math>: that is, the decision maker attains a higher expected utility under  <math> \sigma </math> than under <math> \sigma' </math> for any utility function.
#There exists a [[Markov kernel | stochastic map]] <math>\gamma </math> such that <math>\sigma'(s' | w) = \sum_{s \in S} \gamma(s, s') \sigma(s | w) </math>: that is,  <math> \sigma' </math> is a garbling of <math> \sigma </math>.
# <math>\Phi_{\sigma'} \subset \Phi_{\sigma} </math>: that is, <math>\sigma</math> yields a larger set of feasible strategies than <math>\sigma'</math>.

== Blackwell order ==

=== Definition ===

Blackwell's theorem allows us to construct a [[partial order]] over information structures. We say that <math>\sigma</math> is ''more informative in the sense of Blackwell'' (or simply ''Blackwell more informative'') than <math>\sigma'</math> if any (and therefore all) of the conditions of Blackwell's theorem holds, and write <math>\sigma' \preceq_B \sigma </math>.

The order <math>\preceq_B  </math> is not a complete one, and most experiments cannot be ranked by it. More specifically, it is a [[Total order#Chains|chain]] of the partially-ordered set of information structures.<ref name = "kosenko" />

=== Applications ===

The Blackwell order has many applications in [[decision theory]] and [[economics]], in particular in [[contract theory]]. For example, if two information structures in a [[Principal-agent problem|principal-agent model]] can be ranked in the Blackwell sense, then the more informative one is more efficient in the sense of inducing a smaller cost for [[Theory of the second best|second-best]] [[Implementability (mechanism design)|implementation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grossman |first1=Sanford J. |last2=Hart |first2=Oliver D. |author1-link=Sanford J. Grossman |author2-link=Oliver Hart (economist) |title=An Analysis of the Principal-Agent Problem |journal=Econometrica |date=1983 |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=7–45 |doi=10.2307/1912246 |jstor=1912246 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1912246|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Laffont |first1=Jean-Jacques |last2=Martimort |first2=David |author1-link=Jean-Jacques Laffont |author2-link=David Martimort |title=The Theory of Incentives: The Principal-Agent Model |date=2002 |publisher=Princeton University Press |jstor=j.ctv7h0rwr |isbn=978-0691091846 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv7h0rwr}}</ref>
